## Theory of Regression Analysis {.smaller}

**A full-day workshop for community medicine residents and faculty**

| Time | Session | Topics |
|---|---|---|
| 09:00 – 10:00 | **1 · Foundations** + Lab 1 | What regression is · choosing a model |
| 10:00 – 11:15 | **2 · Simple linear regression** + Lab 2 | Equation · prediction · R² · centering |
| 11:15 – 11:30 | *Tea* | |
| 11:30 – 13:00 | **3 · Inference & multiple regression** + Lab 3 | β, p, CI · confounding · dummy variables · model building |
| 13:00 – 13:45 | *Lunch* | |
| 13:45 – 14:30 | **4 · Assumptions** + Lab 4 | Linearity · independence · normality · variance · collinearity |
| 14:30 – 16:10 | **5 · Logistic regression** + Lab 5 | Odds · likelihood · ROC · OR vs PR |
| 16:10 – 16:25 | *Tea* | |

Walk through the day. Stress that every session ends with a lab in R and a 5-question self-check quiz.
Everyone should have R, the workshop repo and the `data/ncd_survey.csv` file open before we start.
:::

## Our running example {.smaller}

> *"Does eating more salt raise blood pressure in our community — and by how much?"*

::: {.incremental}
- A **simulated** NCD survey: **600 adults aged 30–69** across **20 villages** in an Indian community setting
- Outcomes: **systolic BP** (continuous) and **hypertension** (yes/no)
- Exposure of interest: **daily salt intake** (g/day)
- Other variables: age, sex, residence, education, BMI, waist, tobacco, alcohol, physical activity
- All six sessions and labs use the same dataset
:::

::: {.notes}
The data are simulated so that every teaching point (confounding, collinearity, non-constant variance, clustering, common outcome, missing values) shows up on cue. Do not mention individual features yet — we will discover them.
:::

# Topic 1 — What is regression? {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## What is regression?

::: {.key}
Regression describes how the **average** value of an **outcome** changes with one or more **predictors**.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- "Among adults who eat 8 g of salt a day, the *average* SBP is …"
- "For each extra 1 g/day of salt, average SBP is … mmHg higher"
- One equation gives **description**, **comparison** and **prediction**
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
ggplot(ncd, aes(salt_g, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .35, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red, fill = col_red, alpha = .15) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")
```
:::
:::

## Why do we use regression? {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. **Describe** an association with a number in real units
2. **Adjust** for other factors (age, BMI …) — the key idea in observational public health research
3. **Predict** an outcome for a new person or community
4. **Test** a hypothesis with a confidence interval
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Why not just a t-test or chi-square?**

- They compare groups, one variable at a time
- Regression handles **continuous exposures**, **many variables at once**, and gives an **effect size** (not only a p-value)
:::
:::
:::

## Regression in community medicine {.smaller}

| Public health question | Outcome | Typical model |
|---|---|---|
| Is household wealth associated with child haemoglobin (NFHS)? | Hb (g/dL) – continuous | Linear |
| Which factors predict hypertension in a screening camp? | Hypertension – binary | Logistic |
| Rainfall and monthly dengue cases per ward | Count | Poisson / neg. binomial |
| Stage of diabetic retinopathy and duration of diabetes | Ordered categories | Ordinal logistic |
| Time to treatment failure in DOTS patients | Time-to-event | Cox |
| Blood pressure of patients repeated across visits in one PHC | Repeated measures | Mixed model / GEE |

::: {.notes}
Ask the audience for their own thesis topics and place each on this table. The right-most column is the thread of the whole day.
:::

## Correlation vs regression: same data

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
r <- cor(ncd$sbp, ncd$salt_g, use = "complete.obs")
ggplot(ncd, aes(salt_g, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, colour = col_blue) +
  annotate("label", x = 3, y = 185, hjust = 0, size = 6, fill = "#fef9e7",
           label = paste0("Correlation: r = ", round(r, 2), "\nno 'outcome' vs 'predictor'")) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")
```

## Correlation vs regression: same data

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
b <- coef(lm(sbp ~ salt_g, ncd))
ggplot(ncd, aes(salt_g, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red, se = FALSE) +
  annotate("label", x = 3, y = 185, hjust = 0, size = 6, fill = "#fdedec",
           label = paste0("Regression: SBP = ", round(b[1]), " + ", round(b[2], 1),
                          " x salt\n-> ", round(b[2], 1), " mmHg per g/day")) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")
```

## Correlation vs regression: the differences {.smaller}

```{r}
cor(ncd$sbp, ncd$salt_g, use = "complete.obs")        # symmetric, unit-free
coef(lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = ncd))["salt_g"]           # directional, in mmHg per g
coef(lm(salt_g ~ sbp, data = ncd))["sbp"]              # swap the roles -> a different slope
```

| | Correlation (r) | Regression (β) |
|---|---|---|
| Roles of X and Y | Symmetric | **Outcome** and **predictor** |
| Units | None (−1 to +1) | **Outcome units per predictor unit** |
| Adjust for other variables | No | **Yes** |
| Predict new values | No | **Yes** |

## Dependent vs independent variables {.smaller}

| Role | Also called | In our survey |
|---|---|---|
| **Dependent** variable | outcome, response, Y | SBP, hypertension |
| **Independent** variable | predictor, exposure, X, covariate | salt intake, age, BMI … |
| **Confounder** | adjustment variable | age, BMI (related to salt *and* SBP) |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.warn}
"Dependent" is a **modelling role**, not a statement of causation. The same variable can be an outcome in one analysis and a predictor in another (BMI!).
:::
:::

## Type of outcome decides the model

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Continuous**

- SBP (mmHg), BMI, Hb
- Summarised by mean ± SD
- → **linear regression**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Categorical**

- Binary: hypertension yes/no
- Nominal: facility chosen (PHC / CHC / private)
- Ordinal: BP stage 1 / 2 / 3
- Plus **counts** and **time-to-event**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
The first question in any regression analysis is not "which software?" but **"what type of outcome do I have?"**
:::
:::

# Choosing a model {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## The model-selection flowchart

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 16, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 14, 'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '19px', 'fontFamily': 'Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  Q{{"What type of<br/>outcome<br/>do you have?"}}
  Q --> C["Continuous (SBP, BMI, Hb)"] --> L["Linear regression ✅ S2–4"]
  Q --> B["Binary (HTN yes/no)"] --> LG["Logistic regression ✅ S5"]
  LG -.-> PR["Common outcome → prevalence ratio:<br/>Poisson (robust SE) / log-binomial ✅ S5"]
  Q --> N["Count (cases per ward)"] --> P["Poisson / negative binomial"]
  Q --> O["Ordinal (stage 1–3)"] --> OL["Ordinal logistic"]
  Q --> NM["Nominal (3+ unordered)"] --> M["Multinomial logistic"]
  Q --> T["Time-to-event"] --> CX["Cox regression"]
  Q --> CL["Clustered / repeated<br/>(villages, visits)"] --> MM["Mixed models / GEE<br/>(mention only)"]
  classDef today fill:#d5f5e3,stroke:#27ae60,stroke-width:3px,color:#145a32;
  classDef later fill:#f2f3f4,stroke:#aab7b8,color:#566573;
  class L,LG,PR today;
  class P,OL,M,CX,MM later;
```

::: {.notes}
Green = covered today (linear, logistic and the prevalence-ratio variant). Grey = Session 6 "beyond this workshop" slide gives packages and one line on when to use each. Clustering is not an outcome type but changes how we fit: our villages are an example.
:::

## Flowchart in practice: our survey

| Question | Outcome type | Model | Today? |
|---|---|---|---|
| By how much does SBP change per gram of salt? | Continuous | Linear | <span class="pill">✔ S2–4</span> |
| What are the odds of hypertension per gram of salt? | Binary | Logistic | <span class="pill">✔ S5</span> |
| How many times *more prevalent* is HTN in 50+ vs <50? | Binary, common | Poisson-robust | <span class="pill">✔ S5</span> |
| Number of NCD clinic visits last year | Count | Poisson / NB | <span class="pill no">later</span> |
| Time until a hypertensive starts treatment | Time-to-event | Cox | <span class="pill no">later</span> |
| Villages share unmeasured factors | Clustered | Mixed / GEE | <span class="pill no">mention</span> |

# Meet the data {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Data dictionary {.smaller}

| Variable | Meaning | Type |
|---|---|---|
| `id`, `village` | Participant ID; village (20 clusters) | ID / cluster |
| `age`, `sex`, `residence`, `education` | Demographics (4 education levels) | numeric / categorical |
| `bmi`, `waist` | kg/m², cm | continuous |
| `salt_g` | Daily salt intake (g) | continuous |
| `tobacco`, `alcohol`, `phys_act` | Yes/No; low/moderate/high | categorical |
| `sbp`, `dbp` | Blood pressure (mmHg) | continuous (**outcomes**) |
| `htn` | SBP ≥ 140 **or** DBP ≥ 90 | binary (**outcome**) |

## Import and inspect

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
ncd_raw <- read_csv("../data/ncd_survey.csv")
glimpse(ncd_raw)
```

::: {.notes}
In the lab the path is found automatically from the script. On the slide the deck sits in regression-workshop/ so the relative path is ../data/. Behind the scenes the deck converts text columns to factors with sensible level order (as in Lab 1, Task 4) and keeps the prepared data frame as `ncd`.
:::

## Missing values

```{r}
ncd_raw |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> filter(value > 0)
```

::: {.fragment}
Three variables have about 3% missing. A regression model **silently drops** these rows (complete-case analysis) — so n changes from model to model unless you plan for it.
:::

## Table 1 with `tbl_summary()`

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
library(gtsummary)
ncd |>
  select(age, sex, residence, education, bmi, salt_g, tobacco, alcohol, phys_act, htn_f) |>
  tbl_summary(by = htn_f, missing_text = "(Missing)") |>
  add_overall() |> add_p()
```

::: {.notes}
Point at the Missing rows, the medians for continuous variables and the p-values. Table 1 compares groups one variable at a time: it cannot adjust, and it cannot tell us about causation.
:::

## Look before you model

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
ggplot(ncd, aes(salt_g, sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red) +
  labs(x = "Salt intake (g/day)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")
```

## `cor()` — and its limits

```{r}
ncd |> select(age, bmi, waist, salt_g, sbp) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |> round(2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- `use = "pairwise.complete.obs"` handles the missing values
- `sbp` and `salt_g`: moderate positive correlation — but **age and BMI also correlate with salt**
- `bmi` and `waist`: **r = 0.95**. Remember this — it comes back in Session 4
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q1", "A study asks: *Is tobacco use (yes/no) associated with having hypertension (yes/no), after adjusting for age?* Which model?",
         c("Linear regression", "Logistic regression", "Cox regression", "Poisson regression for counts"), answer = 2,
         explain = "The outcome (hypertension) is binary, so logistic regression is the starting point.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q2", "Time from starting TB treatment to death, with some patients lost to follow-up (censored). Which model?",
         c("Linear regression",
           "Poisson regression",
           "Cox regression",
           "Ordinal logistic"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Time-to-event data with censoring call for Cox regression.")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s1q3", "Which statement about correlation vs regression is TRUE?",
         c("Correlation reports the change in Y per one-unit change in X",
           "Regression treats X and Y interchangeably, like correlation does",
           "Regression gives a slope in units and can include other variables",
           "Swapping X and Y changes the correlation but not the regression slope"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Correlation is symmetric and unit-free. Regression is directional (swapping roles changes the slope), gives an effect in outcome units and can adjust for other variables.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_fill("s1q4", "A study records whether each patient is alive or dead one year after diagnosis. What type of outcome is this? (one word)",
          accept = c("binary", "dichotomous"),
          explain = "Two possible categories means a binary outcome, which points to logistic regression.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_fill("s1q5", "About 3% of salt_g values are missing and a model silently drops those people. What is this default approach called? (two words)",
          accept = c("complete case", "complete-case", "complete case analysis", "complete-case analysis", "listwise deletion"),
          explain = "Analysing only rows with no missing model variable is complete-case analysis, so n can change from model to model.")
```

## Score and take-home {.smaller}

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- Regression = how the **average outcome** changes with predictors, **in real units**
- **Outcome type** → model (flowchart); today = linear and logistic
- Regression ≠ correlation: it has direction, units, adjustment and prediction
- Always **look at the data** first: Table 1, plots, missing values
:::
